item.title: Inside an Exposed ARTEX Workspace
item.description:
An exposed working directory on an ARTEX AI pentest operator's host handed researchers 29 files reconstructing a full JNDI injection test chain, revealing the platform labeled 78 findings "confirmed" while its own logs show zero code execution.
Key findings:
- ThreatMon recovered 29 files (27 distinct SHA-256 values) from an open directory listing on 64.176.34[.]176, the same host running the ARTEX console and callback services. The workspace included round1_calib.py, round2_matrix.py, round3_positions.py, Exploit[.]java, Exploit.class, a hand-written LDAP server (ldap_srv.py), an RMI reference server (RmiRefServer[.]java), and operator notes in SUMMARY[.]md. The Chinese-language web console ran on Next.js, and both godliketrenchan[.]com and www.godliketrenchan[.]com resolved to the same IP. The TLS listener on TCP/443 served a self-issued certificate with common name bf4119-beacon regardless of SNI, fingerprint 07654e9c10b01c9274639a45a2ad1d163edad8405add3dc264b0f52bbaab57e3, a stable pivot for internet-wide certificate searches.
- The operator built a four-service JNDI injection chain: an LDAP server on TCP/11389, an RMI registry on TCP/11099, an HTTP server on TCP/8000 serving Exploit.class (SHA-256: 24724c1acd5fcfe1feccde612e09c283676a19b5e227efcad9e4ab382f6b2f45), and a TCP callback listener on TCP/18080. Exploit.class carried a CLASSLOADED execution marker: if the static initializer ran on the target, it would beacon home. The operator also used DNS-based out-of-band logging via dnsutil[.]py and dns.raw.jsonl, confirmed external reachability through a SOCKS5 exit, and compiled the payload with javac -release 8 for older JDK compatibility. The local LDAP/RMI stack validated successfully, but the local test explicitly enabled com.sun.jndi.ldap.object.trustURLCodebase, a setting disabled by default in current JDKs, which makes local success irrelevant to the external target.
- No CLASSLOADED marker appears in cb.log, ldap.log, or http.stdout. HTTP 500 responses were returned both by test payloads and by a deliberate negative control for the nonexistent class com.example.NotExistFoo4316, so the error code carries no execution signal. LDAP search requests and DNS resolution activity were logged externally but cannot be tied to the target's Java process. MITRE ATT&CK mapping covers T1595.002 (scanning), T1583.001 (domain acquisition), T1587.004 (exploit development), T1608.001 (staging Exploit.class over HTTP), and T1190 (attempted exploitation of a public-facing application, execution not observed).
- The platform produced 78 findings each labeled "confirmed": 5 critical, 33 high, 31 medium, 9 low. All 78 also carry traffic_count = 0, a field the platform does not document. None of these findings relate to the JNDI retest; none was independently validated. The "confirmed" label reflects platform output, not a traceable request-response-execution chain on the target.
- OPSEC failures made the entire workspace recoverable: the directory sat open on the same host as the console, and the certificate's common name bf4119-beacon is a durable fingerprint across internet scan datasets.
Hunt action: Search proxy, firewall, and NetFlow logs for connections to 64.176.34[.]176 on TCP/8000, 11389, 11099, and 18080. Hunt application and request logs for jndi:ldap:// and jndi:rmi:// strings. On any legacy Java runtime in your environment, verify com.sun.jndi.ldap.object.trustURLCodebase and com.sun.jndi.rmi.object.trustURLCodebase are not set to true. The IOC table and file hashes are in the ThreatMon report. For any AI or automated pentest output your team receives, the bar is a traceable request, response, and execution signal tied to the target: "confirmed" from the platform is the start of validation, not the end.

item.title: Famous Chollima APT Group: Major Activities, TTPs, and Simulation
item.description:
North Korean 🇰🇵 Famous Chollima weaponizes the developer hiring pipeline across GitHub, npm, and VS Code to deliver BeaverTail, OtterCookie, and PylangGhost, while fraudulent IT workers maintain insider access at Western employers using US 🇺🇸 laptop farms.
Key details:
- The attack chain starts with fake recruiters on LinkedIn, Fiverr, and Discord (T1566.003) pushing trojanized coding assessments hosted on GitHub, Bitbucket, or GitLab. Repositories average 20,000 to 30,000 lines of legitimate code with a single malicious line buried after hundreds of blank lines or spaces (T1027), and payloads are disguised as font files under /public/fontawesome/ or embedded in .svg assets (T1036.008). Execution triggers include npm lifecycle scripts mapping "prepare" to "npm start" so the payload fires on install (T1204.005), VS Code tasks.json with "runOn": "folderOpen" that run git config core.hooksPath .githooks followed by git checkout master to fire a post-checkout hook delivering platform-specific second stages via curl or wget (T1204.002), and more than 2,500 malicious npm packages, including private ones requiring auth tokens to inspect, linked as dependencies (T1195.001). Staging URLs are Base64-encoded and fetched from legitimate SaaS mock-API services like jsonkeeper[.]com and api.mocki[.]io rather than attacker infrastructure.
- The ClickFix lure (T1204.004) targets crypto job seekers with a fake camera-driver error, instructing Win+X then A to open an elevated PowerShell prompt and paste a command that pulls a ZIP to %TEMP%\vdriverWin[.]zip, expands it, and launches update.vbs, which extracts a bundled Python runtime and starts PylangGhost. PylangGhost's auto[.]py steals browser credentials and session cookies from over 80 extensions including 1Password, NordPass, MetaMask, and Phantom, and communicates over plain HTTP with RC4 encryption prefixed by a 16-byte MD5 checksum and a 128-byte key in the clear.
- OtterCookie checks /proc/cpuinfo on Linux for hypervisor, vmware, virtualbox, qemu, kvm, xen, parallels, and bochs strings (T1497.001) and tags its C2 beacon with "(VM)" or "(Local)" so operators filter sandbox runs. Its remote shell uses socket.io-client upgrading HTTP to WebSocket, receiving "command" events and passing msg.message to child_process.exec with windowsHide: true (T1071.001). A keylogging variant installs node-global-key-listener and screenshot-desktop, writing keystrokes to 1.tmp in a Windows cache folder under the temp directory every second and screenshots as 2.jpeg every four seconds (T1056.001). BeaverTail previously dropped a helper module from the C2 path /node/ and saved it as %USERPROFILE%\store.node to decrypt Chrome credentials (T1555.003).
- The parallel IT worker operation (T1684.001) uses US 🇺🇸 laptop farms where facilitators receive employer-issued hardware, then operatives connect remotely from overseas through residential US 🇺🇸 IPs. Operators redirect shipments by filing false theft reports, claiming last-minute relocations, or routing through staffing firms. In August 2025, US 🇺🇸 sanctions exposed nearly $600K in crypto-to-cash transfers; in October 2026, over 40 laptop farms were shut down and 14 people charged, but operations continue. Infrastructure includes hiring-themed domains like coinbase.talenthiringtool[.]com and krakenhire[.]com, and payload hosts like api.quickcamfix[.]online and api.nvidia-release[.]org. Account creation flows through Astrill VPN with residential proxy egress, and the same exit IPs appear in other North Korean 🇰🇵 operations.
- The PolinRider campaign (March 2026) implanted obfuscated JavaScript in hundreds of GitHub repositories to spread a BeaverTail variant, extending supply chain reach beyond individual job applicants. North Korean 🇰🇵 Famous Chollima weaponizes the developer hiring pipeline across GitHub, npm, and VS Code to deliver BeaverTail, OtterCookie, and PylangGhost, while fraudulent IT workers maintain insider access at Western employers using US 🇺🇸 laptop farms.

Key details:

item.title: [remote] Exasol Database 7.1.30 - command execution
item.description:
Exasol Database 7.1.30 ships a hardcoded SYS credential (sys / exasol) that grants full DBA access and OS command execution via a built-in Python UDF, scoring 8.8 High (CVSS:3.1/AV:A/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H).
- The credential pair sys / exasol is printed in the vendor's own docker-db README under "Connecting to the Database" and appears in two internal CI test scripts at /usr/opt/EXASuite-7/EXAClusterOS-7.1.30/docker/test/. Nothing in the container's init path rotates it, sets a must-change flag, or refuses service until it is changed. The ConfD AuthenticationToken and BucketFS WritePasswd are generated as per-deployment randoms; the most privileged credential is not. CWE-1392 is primary; CWE-94, CWE-798, CWE-78, CWE-1188, and CWE-250 are co-recorded.
- The two-step exploit chain requires no memory corruption or protocol bypass. Leg one: authenticate to the binary SQL service on port 8563 over TLS using the shipped constant. Leg two: issue four SQL statements (CREATE SCHEMA, OPEN SCHEMA, CREATE OR REPLACE PYTHON3 SCALAR SCRIPT with an os.popen body, SELECT) and read stdout back through the ordinary result set. No exfiltration channel is needed because the return value crosses the trust boundary in-band. The executing identity observed was uid=500(exadefusr) gid=500(exausers) groups=500(exausers),0(root); that supplementary root group under the vendor-required privileged container mode is a recognised escalation position, though escalation to uid=0 was not attempted or claimed.
- SYS authority over the SQL layer is the larger half of the impact: every schema, table, view, user, and privilege in the analytical warehouse is readable and writable without touching the script engine at all. An attacker can create additional accounts with chosen privileges, giving a durable second entry point that survives rotation of the factory credential. Availability follows the same authority. A separate smaller finding (not scored here): the BucketFS default bucket has Public=True, allowing unauthenticated read listing; write attempts returned 403 because the bucket WritePasswd is a per-deployment random.
- Detection is weak by design. Every step is legitimate product activity: a TLS handshake, a SYS login, a CREATE SCRIPT, and a SELECT. No [28000] authentication-failed sequence will precede a successful hit with the shipped constant. The highest-value detection signal is script-object creation logged with the creating user and source address; the report notes the default deployment does not surface this. A SYS session originating from an unexpected address is the next-best indicator, but operators who never rotated the credential have no baseline to compare against.
- The docker-db 7 deployment form is end-of-life on CentOS 7 and the vendor states no fix is planned for it. The CVE is pending. A conditional 9.8 Critical reading (AV:N) applies to multi-node --network=host deployments and any deployment where port 8563 is published without a loopback restriction. The full proof-of-concept (Python 3, standard library only, --allow-remote gated) and IOCs are in the report at 0day-rubbish[.]com/blog/exasol-database-default-credential-python-udf-os-popen-rce.
Hunt: enumerate all SCRIPT objects in Exasol system tables (EXA_ALL_SCRIPTS) for PYTHON3 bodies referencing os.popen, os.system, or subprocess. Cross-reference script creation timestamps against known administrator sessions. Rotate the SYS credential immediately; with the factory credential changed and no non-admin account holding script-creation rights, the report states this finding does not arise.

item.title: Widespread Token-Spraying Attacks Target Microsoft 365 Accounts For Email Compromise
item.description:
A global token-spraying BEC campaign hit Microsoft 365 environments across 79 organizations, making 200,000+ login attempts and achieving 497 confirmed account takeovers between July and September 2026, all without ever needing a victim's password.
Key findings:
- The attack chain combined AiTM phishing (fake sign-in pages and device-code phishing lures) with session token theft. Because tokens are issued after a legitimate login and MFA verification, whoever holds the token can replay it against Microsoft 365 services with no MFA challenge. The threat actor automated this replay at scale, and in several cases was inside a compromised environment within minutes of token theft.
- Post-compromise persistence was methodical and multi-layered. Attackers wiped existing MFA registrations and enrolled their own authenticator devices, registered attacker-controlled hardware in Entra ID to enable future token requests, and planted hidden inbox rules to silently divert emails from specific contacts, all classic BEC staging moves designed to survive a password reset.
- The monetization pivot was observed: a compromised mailbox was used to send a payroll-redirect phishing email to an internal target. The legitimacy of the sending address is precisely what makes BEC effective. In this instance the payment does not appear to have been completed, but the infrastructure was ready.
- The Huntress report covers 79 customer organizations and at least 200,000 login attempts. The campaign's global reach and automation suggest the operators had significant token inventory and tooling to manage replay sessions at volume, consistent with a financially motivated, organized BEC group rather than opportunistic activity.
For responders investigating a suspected token replay compromise: start in the Entra ID sign-in logs and look for token replay indicators such as sign-ins from unfamiliar IP addresses or ASNs, "Interrupted" or "Success" sign-in results with no corresponding MFA challenge, and sign-ins arriving in rapid succession from geographically inconsistent locations. Then audit registered MFA methods and Entra-joined devices for entries the legitimate user did not add. Pull every inbox rule for affected mailboxes and flag any rule created during or after the suspicious sign-in window. Revoke all active sessions and reset credentials before restoring MFA to prevent re-entry. The Huntress report recommends Conditional Access Policies scoped to All Users, All Cloud Apps, and All Client App types as the structural control to restrict where replayed tokens can be used.

item.title: 2026-10-09: Pcap of infection from Macfinger Clickfix activity
item.description:
A pcap from a Macfinger ClickFix infection chain is now publicly available for analysis, giving DFIR practitioners a full traffic capture to dissect the delivery and post-infection behavior.
Key details:
- The released file is 2026-10-09-Macfinger-ClickFix-and-infection-traffic.pcap[.]zip, weighing in at 20.7 MB (20,689,369 bytes), captured on Friday, October 9, 2026. The naming convention ties it directly to a Macfinger campaign using a ClickFix lure, the social-engineering technique that tricks users into manually executing malicious commands by presenting fake CAPTCHA or browser-fix prompts.
- ClickFix infections typically generate distinctive early-stage traffic: DNS lookups and outbound connections initiated by user-spawned processes like cmd.exe, PowerShell, or mshta shortly after the lure page is visited. The pcap covers both the ClickFix delivery phase and the downstream infection traffic, making it useful for building a full timeline from lure to payload.
- The zip is password-protected under Malware Traffic Analysis's updated password scheme. The password is no longer the legacy format: check the site's "about" page directly before attempting to extract. Failing to do so wastes time and risks confusion about file integrity.
- For network defenders and threat hunters, pcaps like this are ground truth. You can reconstruct the full URI paths, user-agent strings, JA3/JA4 fingerprints, certificate subject fields, and payload delivery hosts directly from the capture without relying on third-party reporting. Wireshark's Protocol Hierarchy and Export Objects features are the fastest first pass.
Practitioner takeaway: load the pcap and filter on HTTP and DNS activity in the first 60 seconds of the capture to isolate the ClickFix delivery stage, then pivot to any non-browser process making outbound connections to identify the post-execution C2 or payload retrieval. Cross-reference resolved domains and IP destinations against passive DNS and threat intel feeds. IOCs will be embedded in the traffic itself.

item.title: PHP2Shell: One Upload, Full Server
item.description:
PHP2Shell: Two critical CVEs in the PHP runtime itself enable unauthenticated memory disclosure and remote code execution beneath every CMS and framework, affecting all PHP versions back to 5.4 across roughly 70% of the web.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are rated critical and sit in the PHP core engine, firing before any application code executes. PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php (highest risk), php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed are all affected across every PHP version from 5.4 onward. RCE was demonstrated against current WordPress, Drupal, and Joomla container images. A clean, fully patched CMS on a vulnerable PHP runtime is still exposed.
- The attack chain starts with a crafted multipart/form-data upload timed to exhaust memory_limit during session upload-progress handling, a pre-application-code phase. The resulting out-of-memory fatal error skips worker cleanup, leaving three engine-global pointers stale: PS(id) for session ID, BG(unserialize) for unserializer state, and EG(last_fatal_error_backtrace) for error tracking. The worker survives and is reused, still holding freed allocations the attacker can reclaim.
- Bug 1 reads leaked worker memory out of the reclaimed PS(id) allocation and encodes it into the PHPSESSID response cookie, defeating ASLR. Bug 2 abuses the stale BG(unserialize) pointer as a memory-corruption primitive and, chained with Bug 1, achieves unauthenticated RCE. Bug 3 abuses EG(last_fatal_error_backtrace) into a second path toward corruption and RCE. A fourth bug, CVE-2026-109619, is an OPcache type confusion in shared memory caused by a race between process-local and shared allocation trackers, exploitable across workers. The researchers note AI tooling compressed exploit development from months to days.
- App-layer logging may capture nothing because exploitation begins in the multipart parsing phase before application code runs. The report's detection signals: malformed or oversized multipart upload requests paired with memory-limit errors or bursts of HTTP 500s; an oversized or malformed PHPSESSID cookie in a response indicating memory leakage; and a PHP worker spawning a child process during upload parsing before application code executes, which the report calls a high-confidence signal. If a server was running vulnerable PHP before the October 21 patch, assume credentials, tokens, and API keys resident in worker memory are compromised.
- Patched releases are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35, shipped October 21. PHP 8.1 and older have no official fix. Varonis states it found no evidence of compromise in its own portfolio and says customers need no additional action for Varonis products specifically.
Practitioner takeaway: inventory every PHP instance, not just public CMS deployments but bundled appliances and internal tools, because the flaw predates your application stack. On web and proxy logs, hunt for multipart upload requests to the same worker IP or process that are followed immediately by HTTP 500 responses or Set-Cookie headers carrying an unusually long or binary-looking PHPSESSID value. Flag any PHP worker process that spawns a child during upload handling. Rotate secrets on any server that ran PHP before October 21. Patch to the relevant fixed branch as the closing step, not the only one.

item.title: Investigating PHP2Shell after patching
item.description:
Two critical PHP RCE vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, both CVSS 9.2) disclosed 21 October 2026 enable unauthenticated code execution. Patching closes the door but does not evict an attacker already inside.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are memory-safety flaws in the PHP runtime. The first exploits a race between memory exhaustion and request cleanup against an incomplete internal state. The second lets a worker reuse freed memory from a prior request. Both allow pre-auth code execution at the web worker's permission level. Apache mod_php is the highest-priority target: demonstrated exploitation fires before application code runs, bypassing login controls entirely. PHP-FPM and other deployments also need review depending on the specific vulnerability and application conditions. Fixed releases are PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, and 8.5.12.
- The real DFIR concern is the window before the patch. The report draws directly on a prior Exchange investigation where an org patched within days of disclosure, believed the server decommissioned after migrating to Office 365, and then suffered a ransomware attempt nearly a year later. The attacker had planted a webshell during that brief pre-patch window and returned through it long after the underlying flaw was remediated. The same scenario is live for every PHP server exposed before today's patch.
- Hunt web roots, upload directories, and other application-writable paths for unexpected scripts. Compare against trusted release baselines. Attackers disguise file extensions and alter timestamps, so scope the search broadly. Correlate suspicious file paths against web server request logs, PHP error logs, process execution records, and outbound connection logs. Useful signals called out in the report include large form submissions, memory-exhaustion errors, and unexpected shells spawned by web worker processes. Successful webshell execution may return HTTP 200 with no crash, so absence of errors does not mean absence of compromise.
- The companion download from Binalyze includes two draft hunting rules: php_web_worker_shell.yml, a Sigma rule for Linux web workers directly spawning shells, and php_webshell_candidates.yar, a YARA rule matching PHP files that contain both request-input references and code or command execution functions. The report notes these are hunting rules, not definitive PHP2Shell signatures. Legitimate applications can match, obfuscated shells and indirect execution can be missed, and local validation and tuning are required before operational use.
- Do not stop at webshells. If an attacker had execution, also examine associated accounts for credential theft, scheduled tasks and cron jobs, new or modified services, and any secrets accessible to the web worker. Include systems believed retired: verify they are actually offline, not just assumed to be. Preserve evidence before removing suspected shells.
Takeaway: Run YARA against collected PHP files from exposed hosts using php_webshell_candidates.yar, and run the Sigma rule php_web_worker_shell.yml against process telemetry for the exposure window. item.content:encoded:
Two critical PHP RCE vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, both CVSS 9.2) disclosed 21 October 2026 enable unauthenticated code execution. Patching closes the door but does not evict an attacker already inside.

Key findings:

- CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are memory-safety flaws in the PHP runtime. The first exploits a race between memory exhaustion and request cleanup against an incomplete internal state. The second lets a worker reuse freed memory from a prior request. Both allow pre-auth code execution at the web worker's permission level. Apache mod_php is the highest-priority target: demonstrated exploitation fires before application code runs, bypassing login controls entirely. PHP-FPM and other deployments also need review depending on the specific vulnerability and application conditions. Fixed releases are PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, and 8.5.12.

- The real DFIR concern is the window before the patch. The report draws directly on a prior Exchange investigation where an org patched within days of disclosure, believed the server decommissioned after migrating to Office 365, and then suffered a ransomware attempt nearly a year later. The attacker had planted a webshell during that brief pre-patch window and returned through it long after the underlying flaw was remediated. The same scenario is live for every PHP server exposed before today's patch.

- Hunt web roots, upload directories, and other application-writable paths for unexpected scripts. Compare against trusted release baselines. Attackers disguise file extensions and alter timestamps, so scope the search broadly. Correlate suspicious file paths against web server request logs, PHP error logs, process execution records, and outbound connection logs. Useful signals called out in the report include large form submissions, memory-exhaustion errors, and unexpected shells spawned by web worker processes. Successful webshell execution may return HTTP 200 with no crash, so absence of errors does not mean absence of compromise.

- The companion download from Binalyze includes two draft hunting rules: php_web_worker_shell.yml, a Sigma rule for Linux web workers directly spawning shells, and php_webshell_candidates.yar, a YARA rule matching PHP files that contain both request-input references and code or command execution functions. The report notes these are hunting rules, not definitive PHP2Shell signatures. Legitimate applications can match, obfuscated shells and indirect execution can be missed, and local validation and tuning are required before operational use.

- Do not stop at webshells. If an attacker had execution, also examine associated accounts for credential theft, scheduled tasks and cron jobs, new or modified services, and any secrets accessible to the web worker. Include systems believed retired: verify they are actually offline, not just assumed to be. Preserve evidence before removing suspected shells.

Takeaway: Run YARA against collected PHP files from exposed hosts using php_webshell_candidates.yar, and run the Sigma rule php_web_worker_shell.yml against process telemetry for the exposure window. Pull web server access logs and look for POST requests to paths outside normal application routes, especially those returning HTTP 200 without corresponding application session activity. Patch closes CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Finding surviving access requires the investigation.

item.title: PHP2Shell: What This Week Tells Us About the Web We Built
item.description:
PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) achieves unauthenticated RCE and memory disclosure across every PHP version since 5.4, with mass exploitation confirmed in the wild before patches shipped. 54.9 million web properties are in scope.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-109618 abuses how PHP handles an out-of-memory condition while request data is half-initialised. CVE-2026-109619 abuses global state that continues pointing at freed request memory. Both are CVSS v4 9.2, both are pre-auth, and both can read live process memory where database credentials, API keys, and session secrets are stored. Every PHP execution model is affected: PHP-FPM, mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. The OOM weakness was first noticed in 2020 and re-discovered in 2024 but never fixed because exploitation looked impractical. In August 2026, AI-assisted research by Calif and OpenAI collapsed that assumption and produced a working exploit chain.
- The embargo failed on multiple fronts. Amazon's MadPot honeypots recorded exploitation attempts on 17 October, four days before coordinated disclosure. CVE IDs leaked publicly on 20 October. A researcher's proof-of-concept video was published by mistake that evening. Chainguard shipped patched container images more than six hours before the embargo lifted, enabling binary diff analysis of the patch. By 21 October at 02:00 UTC, public exploits were circulating. Exploitation "at scale" against the session upload-progress path was reported that afternoon, and European government sites went dark rather than stay online unpatched.
- Patch availability is uneven and that unevenness is where the real incident risk lives. PHP 8.2 through 8.5 have clean updates (8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, 8.5.12). PHP 7.4 through 8.1 have source backports only, requiring a local build and test cycle. PHP 5.4 through 7.3 have no fix at all. Any internet-facing host still on end-of-life PHP is currently unpatched with no vendor-supported remediation path, and Censys counts roughly 2.58 million internet-facing hosts running PHP.
- The natural attacker outcome is a web shell dropped inside a legitimate, SSL-certified site, giving persistent access that blends with normal traffic. From that foothold the attacker can read process memory for credentials, pivot to cloud accounts linked to the host, phish customers from a trusted domain, and serve malware from a URL that reputation systems score clean. For responders: assume compromise on any internet-facing PHP host that was unpatched and reachable after 17 October, the date Amazon first recorded exploitation.
Practitioner takeaway: The immediate hunt priorities are web shells in document roots, new or modified admin accounts, altered core PHP application files, and unexpected outbound connections from PHP worker processes. Rotate every secret that could reside in PHP process memory on an exposed host: database credentials, API keys, cloud access keys, and signing secrets. For hosts on PHP 7.3 and older where no patch exists, isolate from the internet or enforce WAF rules for the known PHP2Shell vectors before treating the asset as a long-term rebuild. Inventory is the forcing function: the organisations that answered "where do we run PHP" in minutes were patched within hours; those still discovering their estate are discovering it in the same order attackers are. The Orca report includes detection details and host-reachability context; the PHP Foundation advisory and Calif's writeup cover the full technical chain.

item.title: How to Identify Compromised eMudhra Certificates With Qualys (CVE-2026-111943 and CVE-2026-111944)
item.description:
CVE-2026-111943 and CVE-2026-111944: Eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates carry fatally weak P-384 keys, enabling private-key recovery and fraudulent cert issuance. Chrome, Mozilla, Apple, and Microsoft have blocked them; your environment may still trust them.
Key findings:
- The root cause is a flaw in a key generation ceremony held April 30, 2025, for 24 subordinate CAs. A wrap/unwrap step produced a second set of weak P-384 keys, reducing effective entropy to an estimated 3 to 8 bits, making private-key recovery trivial to compute. Six of the eight affected intermediates are TLS CAs; two are code-signing CAs. Google removed emSign ECC Root CA - G3 from the Chrome Root Store entirely. eMudhra states its root CA private keys and other intermediates are not affected, and that no leaf certificates were issued to websites or end users under the compromised intermediates.
- The eight affected intermediates span eMudhra BV (G3B) and eMudhra Inc (G3C) and cover EV/OV/DV TLS and OV code-signing roles. Reliable identifiers for each are their SHA-256 fingerprints and serial numbers, all listed in the report. Example: EM EV TLS CA - G3B carries serial c7c41efe92d825f05eae841a4a82c1 and fingerprint E7568FE6E12331F4FD7DE61DA4C7559D0F8EB192A218D4741A3BA75184333838.
- Go runtimes are a distinct exposure path. Go 1.27.3 and 1.26.10 block chains containing the compromised keys under CVE-2026-111943. Older Go versions will still accept those chains. The report notes that unmanaged endpoints and custom trust stores that do not receive automatic distrust updates remain at risk regardless of browser-level blocks.
- Revocation is not a complete control. eMudhra has revoked all eight intermediates, but clients that skip revocation checks can still accept a chain containing them. Confirming that CRL and OCSP checks are functioning correctly is a required response step, not optional hygiene.
Hunt. The issuer-organization query is certificate:(issuer.organization:eMudhra BV or issuer.organization:eMudhra Inc) and the serial-number query targets all eight compromised intermediates individually. For Go runtime exposure, the report ties QID 5019897 to affected Go versions. For certificate chain enumeration on hosts, QID 48395 (eMudhra Intermediate CA Certificates Enumeration) covers assets presenting or using chains containing the compromised intermediates. Any leaf certificate whose chain includes one of the eight should be reissued by a different trusted CA and redeployed before trusting revocation status alone to protect users. The eight SHA-256 fingerprints and serial numbers are in the report.

item.title: BlackX UEFI Bootkit Bypasses Secure Boot on Patched Windows Systems Missing Revocations
item.description:
APT41-linked BlackX UEFI bootkit targets Central Asian-linked espionage campaign, exploiting a 2022 Secure Boot flaw still viable on patched systems that skipped manual revocation steps.
Key findings:
- BlackX is an evolved version of BlackLotus, exploiting CVE-2022-21894 (CVSS 4.4), the "Baton Drop" Secure Boot bypass. The critical gap: Windows updates alone do not block exploitation. Organizations must manually add the "Windows Production PCA 2011" certificate to the UEFI Forbidden List (DBX). Kaspersky confirms the certificate expired October 19, 2026, but expired does not mean blocklisted. Vulnerable binaries still load on systems missing the DBX update, and APT41 appears to have specifically targeted this gap in enterprise patching awareness.
- Infection begins post-compromise with administrator access. The installer drops inst.exe and an encrypted extensionless file PVMDIJGKAX2 to C:\ProgramData\Intel\, launched via command line with an RC4 decryption key as the argument. The binary then writes files to both system and UEFI partitions, installs Machine Owner Keys (MOK), and loads arbitrary EFI files, bypassing Secure Boot entirely. The source code of BlackLotus was never public, meaning APT41 either reverse-engineered or purchased the original to build BlackX, a rare crimeware-to-APT technology transfer.
- Post-exploitation is layered. A kernel driver signed by "Wenjiang District Mingyu Network Technology Service Studio" (certificate now revoked) is injected via the UEFI payload. The driver attempts to tamper with endpoint security, with specific routines targeting Kaspersky and Avast, though Kaspersky's analysis found these ineffective. A RAT using Google Drive, OneDrive, and Yandex.Disk for C2 exfiltrates files and harvests system info. A malicious DLL, OxiDLLRunner, is sideloaded by a delivered googleupdate.exe, decrypting a Rust payload that beacons to archivetj[.]com for additional DLL plugins.
- Attribution to APT41, specifically the FishMonger cluster (also tracked as Aquatic Panda and Earth Lusca), rests on two overlapping indicators: the string "xdd" appearing in both BlackX and a FishMonger kernel implant documented in an ESET June 2026 report, and the DLL sideloading pattern characteristic of Chinese 🇨🇳 threat actors. Diplomatic targets in Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, and Turkmenistan align with documented APT41 espionage priorities against high-value government networks.
- DFIR takeaway: On any host where BlackX is suspected, recovery cannot stop at the OS layer. UEFI partition forensics are required. Look for unauthorized MOK entries and unexpected EFI binaries. Verify DBX state against Microsoft's published revocation list. Hunt for inst.exe and PVMDIJGKAX2 under C:\ProgramData\Intel\, googleupdate.exe outside its expected install path, and unsigned or revoked kernel drivers loaded at boot. Network-side, flag cloud storage C2 patterns and outbound connections to archivetj[.]com. The Kaspersky report contains IOCs.

item.title: Obstacles to Weaponizing PHP2Shell Likely Constrain Immediate Widespread Exploitation
item.description:
PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) discloses two critical RCE flaws in PHP affecting versions before 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, and 8.5.12. No confirmed exploitation in the wild yet, but weaponization attempts are already underway.
Key findings:
- Three distinct memory-corruption flaws underpin PHP2Shell. CVE-2026-109618 is a partial HashTable insertion bug: if a memory allocation fails mid-parse of HTTP request variables, PHP may update its entry count before the corresponding bucket is fully initialized, then attempt to access or release that invalid data at request shutdown, enabling memory corruption or arbitrary code execution. CVE-2026-109619 covers two separate use-after-free conditions tied to cross-request worker state: a serialization-context UAF triggered when zend_bailout() interrupts serialize() or unserialize() and leaves a stale pointer alive into the next request, and a session upload-progress UAF where a fatal error during multipart processing skips session cleanup, again leaving live pointers in a persistent worker.
- The worker reuse model is the forensic thread to pull. Both mod_php and PHP-FPM reuse long-running worker processes across requests. Exploitation of the UAF flaws depends on a subsequent request hitting the same corrupted worker. That means exploitation evidence may appear across two separate HTTP requests in access logs, not a single obvious payload, and worker crashes (PHP-FPM pool restarts, Apache worker segfaults) are a key indicator to correlate with inbound request patterns.
- CrowdStrike Counter Adversary Operations reproduced RCE but has not observed successful wild exploitation or a fully weaponized public exploit. What has been observed is testing, probing, and failed exploitation attempts. POC code circulating now is largely crash-only. Converting crash POCs to reliable RCE requires knowing the exact PHP version, libc, SAPI, and application stack, including specific Docker image releases. This is a meaningful barrier to mass exploitation but not to targeted attacks against known deployment profiles.
- Older and end-of-life PHP versions are also impacted. PHP powers roughly 70% of all websites, including WordPress deployments, making the potential scope enormous if a reliable public exploit emerges. The report notes AI-assisted vulnerability research is accelerating the discovery-to-exploit timeline, and the media attention around PHP2Shell will likely drive additional PHP vulnerability research in the near term.
- Disabling session.upload_progress.enabled in php.ini blocks the upload-progress paths for the two UAF conditions in CVE-2026-109619 but does not address the HashTable flaw in CVE-2026-109618. Restricting request body size, parameter-name length, nesting depth, and form field count at the reverse proxy or WAF layer before requests reach PHP reduces the attack surface for the HashTable parsing bug. After patching, rebuild container images and restart all Apache and PHP-FPM workers to eliminate any stale in-memory state.
Hunt priority: pull PHP-FPM pool error logs and Apache error logs for segfaults and worker restarts, then cross-reference timestamps with access logs for requests containing abnormally long parameter names, deeply nested form fields, or multipart bodies triggering upload-progress handling. IOCs and CrowdStrike's analysis context are in the report.

item.title: PHP2Shell: How to Stay Ahead of a Zero-Day, from Asset Discovery to Threat Hunting
item.description:
PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) are unauthenticated RCE zero-days in PHP itself, affecting every release back to 5.4, with exploitation confirmed four days before the October 21st patch shipped.
Key findings:
- Both CVEs sit in the PHP runtime, not in any application layer. CVE-2026-109618 is an out-of-memory condition during request setup that can produce code execution or leak server memory back in the response. CVE-2026-109619 is a stale-reference-after-free bug where subsequent worker requests can access freed memory, with PHP's session upload progress feature confirmed as one exploitation path. Every PHP deployment mode is affected: PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. Updating WordPress or Drupal does nothing; the runtime itself must be patched to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35.
- Exploitation was observed in honeypot infrastructure by Amazon on October 17th, four days before a patch existed. Cloudflare reported thousands of attempts in the 10 hours before public announcement, jumping to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes after. Government and commercial services across Japan 🇯🇵, the United States 🇺🇸, the United Kingdom 🇬🇧, the Netherlands 🇳🇱, Finland 🇫🇮, France 🇫🇷, Denmark 🇩🇰, Germany 🇩🇪, and Brazil 🇧🇷 went offline as a precaution, with payroll and national identity services among those disrupted.
- Application logs and WAFs frequently miss these exploits because the flaws trigger before application code runs. The ExtraHop report highlights a critical detection finding: the most dangerous CVE-2026-109618 requests were not readable as well-formed HTTP, making transaction-level rules blind to them. Connection-level analysis, comparing total bytes a client sent against what was parseable as HTTP, caught them. In lab replay across 263 attack connections, the server's share of traffic was under 0.06%, because PHP sends nothing until it has read the full flood. Attack packet sizes ran 74-117 bytes; normal large uploads ran about 1,430. Status codes also mislead: the same crash returns either a 500 or a 200 depending on PHP error settings.
- The report lays out concrete network-observable signatures defenders can hunt in stored traffic covering the pre-patch window. Look for: client connections to web servers that sent more than 1 MB in small packets and received almost nothing back; bursts of multipart requests carrying the PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS field from a single client; Set-Cookie PHPSESSID values longer than 256 characters or containing characters outside any valid PHP session ID format; request URIs or query strings containing sess_ paths or ../ traversal toward session directories. A Session File Include detection that returns a 200 response is the strongest network-level indicator that code actually executed.
- Post-exploitation pivots are where the real damage lands. Once a web shell is planted, attackers move to back-end databases and identity infrastructure. The report flags watching for new outbound connections from web servers, anomalous base64-encoded commands in headers, and non-standard SSH, RDP, or SMB credential-dumping activity originating from web servers that match the patterns above. Kerberos, NTLM, and LDAP traffic from a compromised web server to domain controllers is a high-priority escalation signal.
Practitioner takeaway: Do not limit your retrospective to post-patch dates. Exploitation predated the patch by at least four days. The web server is the entry point, not the target.

PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) are unauthenticated RCE zero-days in PHP itself, affecting every release back to 5.4, with exploitation confirmed four days before the October 21st patch shipped.

Key findings:

- Both CVEs sit in the PHP runtime, not in any application layer. CVE-2026-109618 is an out-of-memory condition during request setup that can produce code execution or leak server memory back in the response. CVE-2026-109619 is a stale-reference-after-free bug where subsequent worker requests can access freed memory, with PHP's session upload progress feature confirmed as one exploitation path. Every PHP deployment mode is affected: PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. Updating WordPress or Drupal does nothing; the runtime itself must be patched to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35.

- Exploitation was observed in honeypot infrastructure by Amazon on October 17th, four days before a patch existed. Cloudflare reported thousands of attempts in the 10 hours before public announcement, jumping to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes after. Government and commercial services across Japan 🇯🇵, the United States 🇺🇸, the United Kingdom 🇬🇧, the Netherlands 🇳🇱, Finland 🇫🇮, France 🇫🇷, Denmark 🇩🇰, Germany 🇩🇪, and Brazil 🇧🇷 went offline as a precaution, with payroll and national identity services among those disrupted.

- Application logs and WAFs frequently miss these exploits because the flaws trigger before application code runs. The ExtraHop report highlights a critical detection finding: the most dangerous CVE-2026-109618 requests were not readable as well-formed HTTP, making transaction-level rules blind to them. Connection-level analysis, comparing total bytes a client sent against what was parseable as HTTP, caught them. In lab replay across 263 attack connections, the server's share of traffic was under 0.06%, because PHP sends nothing until it has read the full flood. Attack packet sizes ran 74-117 bytes; normal large uploads ran about 1,430. Status codes also mislead: the same crash returns either a 500 or a 200 depending on PHP error settings.

item.title: Exposed Infrastructure Reveals How Ransomware Affiliates Used AI Agents to Execute Intrusions
item.description:
Russian-speaking ransomware affiliates ran a partially AI-executed intrusion operation across 62 organizations, with INC and The Gentlemen groups benefiting. Exposed infrastructure at 45.227.254[.]43 revealed the full kill chain, toolkit, and victim tracking system.
Key findings:
- The core framework, Phantom, is an AI-powered offensive platform deployed via OpenCode using OpenRouter-hosted commercial models. It supports 18 skill modules covering reconnaissance, EDR fingerprinting, exploit research, and steganography. When AI models declined a prompt, the operator reworded the request as an authorized red team assessment rather than switching models. Logged activity shows 8,257 messages across 133 sessions. The operation uses an "AI-executed, human-approved" structure: the human provides a victim prompt and approves each step, but execution is automated.
- CVEs actively exploited in the campaign include CVE-2024-57727 (SimpleHelp path traversal) and CVE-2026-35616 (Fortinet FortiClient authentication bypass) and CVE-2026-41940 (cPanel/WHM authentication bypass). CVE-2026-15409 (SonicWall SMA 1000 SSRF) was staged for targeting with no confirmed compromise. CVE-2026-63030 (WordPress wp2shell), CVE-2026-42208 (LiteLLM SQL injection), and CVE-2026-9082 (Drupal SQL injection) were developed or referenced in operator records.
- Post-access tradecraft followed a consistent lifecycle: domain enumeration, escalation to domain admin, credential harvesting with stealer tooling, and prioritized collection of finance, HR, legal, and executive files over reverse-SOCKS tunnels using RevSocks. In one documented case, a single reused password unlocked VPN, servers, RMM, backup, and security management platforms simultaneously. Security products were impaired using a BYOVD attack abusing the Zemana driver (zam64.sys) via a Quick Heal/Seqrite EDR killer. Operator logs record mixed results against enterprise EDRs.
- The toolkit also includes WormGPT-MCP (32 MCP servers spanning reconnaissance through extortion), Ghost C2 (three generations of polymorphic implants communicating over Cloudflare, Telegram, or DNS), a Cloudflare-fronted Mythic agent called QuickLine, and exfiltration tools rks3 and BackupAgent. AI-authored extortion records show the actors analyzed stolen financials to calibrate ransom demands below insurance or banking thresholds, then applied pressure through vishing calls and regulatory notification threats with 24-72 hour deadlines.
- Scope: 62 organizations targeted, four confirmed on INC and The Gentlemen leak sites. The US 🇺🇸 accounts for more than 50% of targets. Industrial, manufacturing, and energy sectors were hit hardest, followed by healthcare and pharmaceutical organizations.
Practitioner takeaway: the exposed directory at 45.227.254[.]43 is the starting point for infrastructure pivoting. Hunt your perimeter logs for exploitation attempts against FortiClient EMS gateways, SimpleHelp RMM servers, and cPanel endpoints tied to these CVEs. Internally, look for zam64.sys loaded by unexpected processes as a BYOVD indicator, reverse-SOCKS tunnel activity, and lateral movement patterns where a single credential authenticates across VPN, RMM, and backup platforms in short succession. The SOCRadar report is the primary source for operator TTPs documented from the exposed infrastructure.

item.title: PHP2Shell Operational Guidance
item.description:
Two critical PHP RCE flaws, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (both CVSS v4.0 9.2), dubbed PHP2Shell, are under active exploitation attempts across internet-facing PHP deployments worldwide, with no confirmed successful compromise yet.
Key details:
- CVE-2026-109618 triggers RCE via out-of-memory corruption; CVE-2026-109619 via stale global state. Both allow unauthenticated RCE across PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. Apache mod_php is the highest-priority target: unauthenticated exploitation has already been demonstrated. A third flaw, CVE-2026-115560 (RCE, lower severity), was disclosed 23 October and will ship in the regular release cycle; its mitigation overlaps with CVE-2026-109619.
- Amazon's MadPot honeypot logged the first exploitation attempt on 17 October, four days before public disclosure. Amazon, Cloudflare, WatchTowr, and NVISO all confirm active exploitation attempts. Exploitation attempts began crashing servers, indicating probe-and-crash behavior from immature exploits. VulnCheck claims a working exploit for CVE-2026-109618 but this has not been independently confirmed. Over 748 GitHub repositories referencing PHP2Shell exist, some with over a thousand stars, but no publicly available exploit has been confirmed to reliably achieve stable code execution due to the need to bypass ASLR simultaneously.
- For CVE-2026-109618 where patching is delayed: set memory_limit=-1 via php_admin_value in FPM pool or Apache config (not overridable by application), set post_max_size to 8M (no uploads) or 32M (uploads required), and enforce request size, field count, multipart part count, header count, and nesting depth limits at the web server or proxy layer. Do not use RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA as substitutes; these can trigger the vulnerable allocation path. For CVE-2026-109619: set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and restart every worker via php.ini, FPM pool, or server config; on PHP 8.5 additionally set fatal_error_backtraces=0 and restart workers.
- Patch targets: PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, 8.2.35. PHP 8.1 and older receive no upstream fix; vendor backports or migration are required. Critically, updating a CMS like WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, or Magento does NOT update the underlying PHP runtime. Verify the actual runtime version in production after patching, including in load-balanced nodes, containers, and staging environments.
DFIR takeaway: Treat pre-patch windows as potential compromise windows. Hunt for php-fpm, php-cgi, apache2, or httpd spawning sh, bash, curl, or wget as child processes. Review HTTP access logs and reverse-proxy telemetry for unusual request patterns or spikes in 500-series errors around 17-21 October 2026, before patches were available. Audit web-accessible directories for newly created or modified PHP files indicating webshell staging. Where suspicious activity is found, preserve telemetry before remediation overwrites state. The NVISO report includes PHP-specific mitigation configuration steps in full.

item.title: AI-Assisted Cyberespionage Campaign Targets Government Systems
item.description:
Unattributed cyberespionage cluster CL-UNK-1211 hit government entities with AI-assisted payloads, custom Go RAT, and deep anti-forensics across a six-month Linux-focused campaign targeting databases and email.
Key findings:
- SysGoRAT, a Go-based RAT initially observed as sys-control-client and also masquerading as pip2.7, ea_install, and semanage, communicates over WebSocket to a hardcoded C2 at 104.194.158[.]65:443. It supports six persistence methods: systemd (installs sys-update.service), cron at five-minute intervals, registry Run keys, and scheduled tasks using OneDrive-themed identifiers on Windows. Its cross-platform design also provides TCP proxy and interactive shell capability, making it a full post-exploitation platform, not just a backdoor.
- Initial persistence was established by hijacking the auto_prepend_file directive in PHP configs under /etc/php/ and /opt/plesk/php/, forcing malicious code to execute before every legitimate PHP request. A web shell planted at /usr/lib/php/plesk_sys_driver.php impersonated Plesk infrastructure. SSH persistence followed via unauthorized keys in authorized_keys files, SUID-enabled binaries, and modified system binaries. Credential harvesting used a .bashrc sudo alias that silently logged passwords to a file named Solarwinds.StatusLog.txt to blend with SolarWinds artifacts. No SolarWinds compromise was found.
- Lateral movement ran through SSH with harvested creds, MSSQL xp_cmdshell for OS command execution, and a double-hop SQL chain to reach segregated network segments. Tunneling used revsocks, pysoxy, and GSocket. Reverse shells via Bash, Python, and Netcat contacted at least seven distinct C2 servers. A custom Go scanner targeted CVE-2025-55182 (React2Shell) for internal reconnaissance. Privilege escalation used LinPEAS and a CVE-2021-4034 PwnKit exploit attempt (hash: 44e83f84a5d5219e2f7c3cf1e4f02489cae81361227f46946abe4b8d8245b879).
- Data targeting focused on government mailboxes and databases. A script named search_social.php extracted email headers linked to Facebook, Instagram, Twitter, TikTok, and LinkedIn accounts. Database records were dumped to CSV, compressed, and staged for transfer via transfer[.]sh, bashupload[.]com, filebin[.]net, and the catbox[.]moe API. Anti-forensics included timestomping with touch -t, log deletion across auth, web, and OS logs, immediate post-execution script removal, and planted red-team markers including RedTeamOps2025 and pentest123 to mimic authorized testing activity and misdirect responders.
- Multiple PHP and shell scripts carried conversational annotations and step-by-step reasoning comments consistent with LLM-generated code, though Unit 42 could not confirm autonomous AI execution. The campaign remains unattributed, with nation-state and financial motivations both considered. Three samples are in the PolySwarm report: GsNetcat (d94f75a70b5cabaf786ac57177ed841732e62bdcc9a29e06e5b41d9be567bcfa), the PwnKit exploit above, and a PHP web shell (1505a3a727f8899b2ad343519f7bf9c438b8b802f8d6b854f5db3b52f857c76a).
Practitioners investigating Linux servers should prioritize centralized log sources over host-resident artifacts: this actor deleted auth logs, web logs, and bash histories aggressively. Hunt for auto_prepend_file modifications in PHP ini files, unexpected entries in authorized_keys, SUID binaries outside standard paths, processes named sys-update.service or cron entries with five-minute intervals, and outbound WebSocket connections on port 443 to unfamiliar IPs. The planted RedTeamOps2025 marker is a deliberate misdirection; do not dismiss anomalous activity on that basis alone. IOCs and sample hashes are in the report.

item.title: Enter 666: Unmasking Beast Ransomware
item.description:
Beast Ransomware, a RaaS operation attributed to actor Hyadina and linked to the later GodDamn variant, combines a GUI-driven affiliate interface with layered ChaCha20/Curve25519 encryption and aggressive recovery inhibition across Windows, NAS, and ESXi targets.
Key findings:
- The analyzed sample (SHA-256: 4c44ac1eea4bc7f4ea542d611b5658d7ac2729d79abe750da83f1581cd832eaf) is an 81 KB PE32 executable compiled 2024-08-09. Strings are stack-assembled and XOR-decoded in place with a single-byte key of 0x55, and the embedded config blob is ChaCha20-encrypted in the .data section, with the key and nonce stored immediately before it, making it recoverable via static analysis. A builder check for the literal strings !!!CONFIG!!! and !!!PASSWORD!!! can fingerprint unfinished or template payloads. The mutex BEAST HERE? provides a single-instance guard detectable in handle or memory telemetry early in execution.
- Beast phones home to iplogger[.]co/1v1i85.torrent twice per infection, passing the victim GUID in the User-Agent header and BEGIN or END in the Referer to bookend the encryption window. This gives the operator remote confirmation of execution without a traditional C2 channel. The ransomware also applies geographic exclusion via GetSystemDefaultUILanguage and GetLocaleInfoW, skipping a hardcoded list of CIS and associated country locales.
- Persistence lands at HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run with the victim GUID as the value name, requiring no admin rights. When the -I flag is active, Beast relocates itself to %ALLUSERSPROFILE%\{victim-GUID}\<8 random letters>.exe before writing that key, so the persisted binary lives at the relocation path, not the original drop location. The key file default.key, written beside the executable or in %TEMP%, holds the session public key and both attacker-protected copies of the session private key and persists across runs to maintain a consistent victim identifier.
- Encryption uses ChaCha20 with a Curve25519 ECDH key hierarchy: a per-machine session keypair is generated, the session private key is wrapped under two embedded attacker public keys and wiped from memory, then a fresh per-file ephemeral keypair is generated for every file. The 160-byte footer appended to each encrypted file contains everything needed for attacker-side decryption and ends with the 8-byte marker 66 6B EA 57 1A BE 16 66, which Beast uses to skip already-processed files. Encrypted files carry the extension .{victim-GUID}.moon and a ransom note of README.TXT. Intermittent encryption processes 25% of 128 KiB chunks by default, with a minimum of three chunks, capping encrypted volume at 512 MiB for files over 1 GiB.
- Recovery inhibition is layered: 73 services and 52 processes (backup agents, SQL engines, Veeam, Exchange, security products) are killed before encryption begins; Volume Shadow Copies are deleted via WMI ExecQuery and DeleteInstance against Win32_ShadowCopy; the Recycle Bin is emptied with SHEmptyRecycleBin; and the Windows Restart Manager (rstrtmgr.dll resolved at runtime) is used to unlock files held open by processes not on the kill list. Network targeting starts from the ARP cache via GetIpNetTable, probes private /24 subnets on TCP/445, and converts discovered shares to UNC paths for encryption, explicitly excluding ADMIN$.
Hunt tip: correlate three signals together, the HKCU Run key written with a GUID-format value name, an outbound HTTP request to iplogger[.]co with a GUID in User-Agent and BEGIN or END in Referer, and WMI activity against Win32_ShadowCopy. Any one of these alone is worth investigating; all three in sequence on a single host is a Beast infection in progress. The report includes the full IOC table, targeted service and process lists, and excluded filename, extension, and folder lists in the appendix.

- Encryption uses ChaCha20 with a Curve25519 ECDH key hierarchy: a per-machine session keypair is generated, the session private key is wrapped under two embedded attacker public keys and wiped from memory, then a fresh per-file ephemeral keypair is generated for every file. The 160-byte footer appended to each encrypted file contains everything needed for attacker-side decryption and ends with the 8-byte marker 66 6B EA 57 1A BE 16 66, which Beast uses to skip already-processed files. Encrypted files carry the extension .{victim-GUID}.moon and a ransom note of README.TXT. Intermittent encryption processes 25% of 128 KiB chunks by default, with a minimum of three chunks, capping encrypted volume at 512 MiB for files over 1 GiB.

- Recovery inhibition is layered: 73 services and 52 processes (backup agents, SQL engines, Veeam, Exchange, security products) are killed before encryption begins; Volume Shadow Copies are deleted via WMI ExecQuery and DeleteInstance against Win32_ShadowCopy; the Recycle Bin is emptied with SHEmptyRecycleBin; and the Windows Restart Manager (rstrtmgr.dll resolved at runtime) is used to unlock files held open by processes not on the kill list. Network targeting starts from the ARP cache via GetIpNetTable, probes private /24 subnets on TCP/445, and converts discovered shares to UNC paths for encryption, explicitly excluding ADMIN$.

Hunt tip: correlate three signals together, the HKCU Run key written with a GUID-format value name, an outbound HTTP request to iplogger[.]co with a GUID in User-Agent and BEGIN or END in Referer, and WMI activity against Win32_ShadowCopy. Any one of these alone is worth investigating; all three in sequence on a single host is a Beast infection in progress. The report includes the full IOC table, targeted service and process lists, and excluded filename, extension, and folder lists in the appendix.

item.title: Inside the LiteLLM 1.107.0 supply chain compromise: Credential theft through Python startup hooks
item.description:
LiteLLM 1.107.0 supply chain compromise delivered a credential-harvesting payload via Python startup hooks, activating on any Python invocation in an affected environment, not just LiteLLM gateway use.
Key findings:
- The attack began with stolen developer GitHub credentials used to redirect the LiteLLM release workflow to the lookalike repository Berri-AI/litellm instead of the legitimate BerriAI/litellm. A second stolen credential satisfied a production approval gate. The compromised wheel dropped three files: cook.pth, cook[.]py, and sitecustomize[.]py into the Python environment's site-packages library directory, outside the litellm application folder. That placement is the critical DFIR detail: removing the litellm directory alone does not remove the payload. The four SHA-256 hashes covering LF and CRLF variants of cook[.]py and sitecustomize[.]py are in the report's IOC table, alongside per-platform wheel hashes.
- Python startup processing, specifically .pth file execution and sitecustomize import during site initialization (T1546.018), ran the collector the moment any Python process started in the affected environment. No import of LiteLLM was required. cook[.]py Base64-decoded and zlib-decompressed the embedded PRIVCOLLECT program (T1027.013, T1140) before launching it in a daemon thread. A separate Unix loader in sitecustomize[.]py used /tmp/remote_code_loader.lock for single-instance enforcement, then polled a GitHub-hosted dead-drop file at hxxps://raw.githubusercontent[.]com/letters9813/pythonclient-test/main/domain.txt (T1102.001) for a mutable C2 address to retrieve and execute arbitrary Python from /codepy. Second-stage retrieval was not confirmed at analysis time, but the mechanism remained live.
- PRIVCOLLECT ran collection modules across developer and AI tool credentials, Git and package-manager config, AWS/Azure CLI/GCP credential caches, Kubernetes service-account files, Docker config, mounted secrets, AWS and GCP metadata API calls (T1552.005), Chromium and Firefox credential databases (T1555.003), SSH, GPG, and TLS key material (T1552.004), shell and database-client histories, Linux procfs process environments, and two LiteLLM proxy database tables via a Prisma child process targeting LiteLLM_CredentialsTable and LiteLLM_ProxyModelTable. Collected data was serialized to JSON, encrypted with AES-256-CBC under a per-run key, wrapped with an embedded 4096-bit RSA public key using OAEP, staged in a gzip tar with data.bin, key.bin, and hdr.json, then POSTed to hxxp://www.litellm[.]dev/healthcheck with a fixed browser-like User-Agent and an X-SHA256 body checksum. OpenSSL staging used temporary directories prefixed .pc_e_; the post-upload marker /tmp/.pc_once_72129118c59f5636c0bb indicates a completed upload attempt.
- Affected environments include developer workstations, CI/CD agents, build and test containers, and LiteLLM proxy hosts, exactly the systems holding model-provider API keys, cloud workload identities, CI secrets, and source-control tokens. Microsoft Defender Antivirus signatures Trojan:PyPI/Stealer.SA, Trojan:PyPI/LiteLlmSupplyChain.A and .B, and Backdoor:PyPI/LiteLlmSupplyChain.C are available as of October 22. TVM-2026-0003 surfaces exposed endpoints in Defender Vulnerability Management.
Practitioner takeaway: do not invoke python, pip, or any interpreter inside a suspect environment to check for the package; startup alone can trigger collection. Scope exposure by searching installed environments, pip/uv caches, lock files, and container images for litellm-1.107.0 and verify against wheel hashes in the report. Hunt cook.pth (SHA-256 7f191632e7320705d154b85204f1ae546b543acbd7e8861229b76f5042b92bdb or 84dc8c82c0a4a4a62552ef826b49fcc86d1a5c4a5d0f2c06665723f93d129d7d) and the sitecustomize[.]py and cook[.]py hashes in your EDR file events. Check for .pc_e_ prefixed directories and /tmp/.pc_once_72129118c59f5636c0bb as markers of staging and upload. Use the four KQL hunting queries in the report targeting DeviceNetworkEvents for www.litellm[.]dev, DeviceFileEvents for the four startup-file hashes, DeviceProcessEvents for the database child process pattern and OpenSSL .pc_e_ staging, and CloudProcessEvents for pkeyutl activity in /tmp/.pc_ paths. Rotate all credentials reachable from any affected identity from a known-clean machine, and revoke sessions rather than relying on password rotation alone.

item.title: php2shell in the Lab, and Where a SOC Catches It
item.description:
CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (php2shell): unauthenticated RCE in PHP core, CVSS v4.0 9.2 each, fixed October 21. Black Hills InfoSec lab-tested both on Linux and Windows and published two production Sigma rules.
Key findings:
- Two separate memory-corruption bugs, both pre-auth RCE as the web-server user. CVE-2026-109619 is a stale-pointer bug where request-owned data outlives the worker memory it references; a confirmed path is session upload progress, which is where the php2shell name originates. CVE-2026-109618 triggers when PHP hits an out-of-memory condition mid-request and cleanup treats half-built data as valid. Affected SAPIs include mod_php, php-fpm, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. Windows is equally affected: the same core ships in php-cgi.exe behind IIS. Fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. Actively exploitable on Linux with public PoCs; no reliable public Windows RCE exists yet, hardened by CFG and ASLR, but the bug is present.
- The successful Linux exploitation chain produced apache2 (www-data) spawning /bin/sh -c "id" spawning id. That process tree is the durable forensic signal, not the memory corruption itself, which is invisible to EDR. The giant multipart POST, the PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS field, Transfer-Encoding chunked, heap-spray bursts of near-identical form fields, and a Set-Cookie: PHPSESSID= carrying binary or %00 bytes all live in the request body and belong to WAF/proxy visibility, not endpoint telemetry. The one log line the lab did capture at crash time: "Allowed memory size ... in Unknown on line 0" in the Apache error log.
- Failed or mistuned attempts crash the worker instead of executing code. On Linux, Apache logs AH00052: child pid N exit signal Abort (6) for allocator-caught heap corruption and exit signal Segmentation fault (11) for unmapped-memory writes. On Windows the equivalent is WerFault.exe spawning and an Application Error Event ID 1000 as php-cgi.exe recycles. Treat a burst of worker crashes paired with matching web-server error log entries as an attempt-hunt signal, not a standalone alert.
- The critical detection lesson: writing the rule to watch for a web worker spawning a recon binary misses the actual chain. PHP's system() and exec() route through /bin/sh -c, making the recon binary a grandchild. The rule must key on the shell child's command line, not the binary. On Windows the same shape appears: w3wp.exe spawns php-cgi.exe spawns cmd.exe /s /c "whoami" spawns whoami.exe. Read the command off cmd.exe, exactly as you read it off sh -c on Linux. Both Sigma rules published in the report key on web-worker parent, shell child, and a delimiter-bounded recon verb on that shell's command line. Linux rule id: 67afd63c-418f-43a4-a4a9-feae3783a641. Windows rule id: 170d3f2a-5734-4941-99f2-cc8b4a99ebe3.
- One mitigation caveat worth carrying: CVE-2026-115560, a separate lower-severity upload-progress vector, is not fixed in the October 21 releases. A full fix is promised in the next regular release. Keep session.upload_progress.enabled = Off even after you apply the October 21 patches. Also: do not use RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA to cap memory as a workaround; the advisory explicitly warns those make mmap() fail, which triggers the same vulnerable path as CVE-2026-109618. On PHP-on-IIS hosts, check whether the php-cgi.exe worker runs as nt authority\iusr with SeImpersonatePrivilege; if a web shell lands there, privilege escalation toward SYSTEM is a risk to assess, not an assumption.
Takeaway: Hunt for web-worker processes (apache2, httpd, nginx, php-fpm, php-cgi, lsphp, frankenphp, w3wp.exe) spawning sh, bash, or cmd.exe/powershell.exe with a recon verb on the shell's command line. Both Sigma rules, with full parent-process lists, shell-child conditions, and delimiter-bounded recon-verb regexes for Linux and Windows, are published in the Black Hills InfoSec report. Backtest against your own fleet before enforcing; the report flags hostname as the most common benign false positive, and short network-recon verbs like ip and ss warrant the same baseline check.

item.title: Signed, Sealed, and Relayed, NTLM-style: Bypassing LDAP Signing Through Reauthentication
item.description:
NTLM relay bypass defeated LDAP signing on every Windows Server 2016 through 2025 domain controller. Microsoft patched LDAP in October 2026 and SMB in September 2026; both fixes are now available and critical to apply.
- The core technique, called "The LDAP Switcheroo" by SpecterOps, works by establishing a signed LDAP connection to a domain controller using attacker-controlled credentials (or anonymous NTLM SASL where accepted), keeping the resulting session key. The attacker then coerces a victim machine over SMB, relays the victim's NTLM AUTHENTICATE message over that already-signed connection, and packs a malicious LDAP ModifyRequest into the same SASL record. The DC verifies the signature once using the attacker's session key, then switches authorization to the victim mid-record and executes the stacked operation with the victim's privileges. The attacker never learns the victim's session key or password.
- The SMB client's NTLMSSP_NEGOTIATE_SIGN flag, historically the thing that blocked SMB-to-LDAP relay, is exactly what makes this work. Without it set, the DC returns operationsError (0x4DC) and rejects the stacked operation. A WebDAV-coerced victim does not set that flag, so only SMB coercion enables this path.
- The practical impact is full domain and forest compromise from an unauthenticated or low-privilege position. In the SpecterOps walkthrough, relaying a domain controller's machine account (LYS-SRV22$) allowed writing msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity on that machine to grant an attacker-controlled account RBCD rights, leading directly to DCSync. The msDS-KeyCredentialLink attribute (shadow credentials) is a parallel primitive. Both run in a single signed SASL record.
- The root cause lives in LDAP_CONN::ProcessRequestEx. Before the patch, the function verified a SASL record once against the connection's current signing key, then processed every LDAP message inside it sequentially, including messages that arrived after LDAP_CONN::SetSecurityContextAtts had already switched the connection's identity to the victim. The fix adds an identity counter to each connection: LDAP_REQUEST::ReceivedClientData snapshots it when data arrives, LDAP_CONN::SetSecurityContextAtts increments it on a bind, and ProcessRequestEx discards the rest of the SASL record if the two values diverge. KB5126646 (October 13, 2026) carries the LDAP fix; KB5122882 (September 2026) carries the SMB fix.
- The bypass is limited to LDAP on 389/TCP. LDAPS (636/TCP) uses TLS for signing, and Windows does not permit NTLM SASL signing or sealing over an existing TLS connection, so there is no attacker-controlled SASL record to stack the operation into. Channel binding, which only applies to LDAPS, is irrelevant to this path; the tested DC had both signing and channel binding enforced and remained vulnerable over 389/TCP.
Takeaway: Apply KB5126646 to every domain controller immediately. After patching, hunt for evidence of exploitation: look for unexpected writes to msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity or msDS-KeyCredentialLink on domain controller computer objects in Active Directory audit logs, and correlate with LDAP bind events on 389/TCP where the binding account differs from the account that appears in the subsequent modify. SpecterOps is releasing the proof-of-concept tool wrapping ntlmrelayx[.]py at github[.]com/grayhatkiller/switcheroo; expect active exploitation attempts shortly. Blocking inbound 389/TCP to domain controllers where operationally feasible and enforcing both LDAP signing and channel binding together remain the layered controls that survive a missed patch.

item.title: How CVE-2026-73570 turns a Zimbra log file into remote code execution
item.description:
CVE-2026-73570 is an unauthenticated RCE in Zimbra that weaponizes a log file: one malformed SMTP address triggers shell execution as the zimbra user, giving an attacker read access to every mailbox and the ability to send as any local identity.
Key findings:
- The injection chain is: malformed RCPT TO -> /var/log/zimbra.log -> Swatchdog pattern match -> Perl dosnmp backtick -> /bin/sh. The attacker sends an SMTP message with an unclosed angle bracket in the recipient address. Postfix rejects it but logs the raw address, which the attacker has crafted to match the service status pattern "Service status change: localhost $(command) changed from stopped to running". Swatchdog tails the log, matches that pattern, and passes the SERVICE field directly into a backtick expression inside the dosnmp Perl subroutine in swatchrc[.]in. No authentication required, no prior foothold needed, just a TCP connection to port 25.
- The vulnerability lives in the perlcode block at line 26 of swatchrc[.]in, specifically the dosnmp function where $args{SERVICE} is interpolated unescaped into a backtick shell call: backtick $snmptrap $snmpsvctrap $snmpsvcname s args{SERVICE} $snmpsvcstatus i $statuses{args{STATUS}} backtick. The zimbra user (uid=997 in Elastic's lab) runs the resulting command with membership in the zimbra and postfix groups, giving full mailbox read, mail relay as any local identity, and likely LDAP and signing key access.
- Elastic Security Labs confirms active exploitation is feasible and that several public PoCs fail because they write incorrectly formatted log entries that Swatchdog never matches, so a failed PoC test can look like a patched server. Their working PoC uses an out-of-band curl callback to confirm execution without leaving additional on-disk artifacts. The 501 SMTP rejection is expected and does not indicate failure; the log write already happened.
- Patch status: Zimbra 10.1.20 (Daffodil release) is the complete fix. The Elastic Security Labs report confirms the vulnerability was reproduced on Release 10.1.16.BETA.4200001.UBUNTU24.64. If you run internet-facing Zimbra SMTP and have not reached 10.1.20, this is pre-auth RCE on port 25 with a public PoC chain confirmed to work.
- The Elastic report ships the detection rule "Zimbra Swatchdog SNMP Command Injection Execution" as a sequence query: it first looks for a shell (sh, bash, dash, ash, zsh, ksh) spawned by a perl parent whose command line matches .swatchdog_script. and contains snmptrap, zmservicename, and zmservicestatus, then correlated by process.entity_id it looks for any child of that shell where process[.]name != snmptrap. That second process is your payload. The rule is retroactive, so you can hunt pre-patch exploitation in historical EDR telemetry.
Responder action: Run the sequence rule against your Linux EDR telemetry going back to your earliest Zimbra logs. If you find hits, treat the zimbra account as fully compromised and scope for mailbox exfil, phishing relay from the server, LDAP exports, and signing key theft. The report calls out local databases and signing keys explicitly as post-exploitation targets beyond the mail store. IOCs and the detection rule are in the Elastic Security Labs report.
